samples.prompt: Describe a place you would like to visit but have not yet been to. You should say: where it is, why you want to visit, what you would do there, and explain why this place interests you.
samples.modelAnswer:
A place I'd really love to visit one day is the city of Kyoto in Japan. I've been interested in Japanese culture since I was a teenager — the architecture, the food, the way design seems to value restraint and beauty in equal measure — and Kyoto somehow embodies all of that more than any other city I've read about.

I know Kyoto used to be the imperial capital for over a thousand years, so it's full of temples, traditional gardens and old wooden houses in the Gion district. What attracts me most is actually the contrast: it's a working modern city with millions of people, but you can step from a busy street into a quiet temple courtyard in a few seconds.

If I went, I'd want to spend at least a week there. I'd visit Kinkaku-ji, the Golden Pavilion, and walk through the bamboo grove at Arashiyama. I'd try to time my visit for either cherry blossom season in early April or for the autumn maple colours in November, because the city is meant to be at its most beautiful then. I'd also love to eat in a traditional kaiseki restaurant — a slow, multi-course meal where every dish is plated like a small piece of art.

What fascinates me about Kyoto is the sense of layered history. People have been refining the same crafts there for centuries — pottery, calligraphy, tea ceremony — and I think experiencing that in person would be very different from just reading about it.
keyPhrases: I've been interested in… since I was a teenager
I'd want to spend at least a week there

samples.prompt: Describe a skill you have learned recently. You should say: what the skill is, how you learned it, how long it took, and explain how the skill has been useful to you.
samples.modelAnswer:
A skill I picked up over the last year is touch-typing — being able to type without looking at the keyboard. It sounds basic, but I'd been hunt-and-pecking with two fingers for most of my life, and it was finally costing me too much time at work.

I started learning through a free online course called Keybr, which throws random letter combinations at you and gradually introduces every key on the keyboard. The first two weeks were quite painful — my speed dropped to maybe ten words a minute, which was much slower than my old method, and I had to consciously stop myself from looking down. There were moments when I genuinely wondered whether it was worth carrying on.

It took about three months of practising fifteen or twenty minutes most days before touch-typing became more natural than my old approach. After about six months I'd reached around sixty words per minute with reasonable accuracy, and today I'd say I sit comfortably between seventy and eighty, which is a meaningful improvement.

The skill has been useful in two main ways. The first is obvious — I can write emails, take notes in meetings and draft documents much faster than before, which probably saves me several hours a week over the course of a working month. The second is less obvious but just as important: because I no longer have to think about which key is where, my attention stays on the actual content of what I'm writing. Ideas flow more directly, which has genuinely improved the quality of my writing too.
keyPhrases: picked up over the last year
wondered whether it was worth carrying on

samples.prompt: Describe a book or a film that influenced you. You should say: what it is, when you read or watched it, what it is about, and explain how it influenced you.
samples.modelAnswer:
A book that genuinely stuck with me is 'Thinking, Fast and Slow' by Daniel Kahneman. I read it about three years ago, during a long train journey across Europe — I picked it up almost by accident in an airport bookshop because someone had recommended it years earlier.

The book is essentially about how human beings actually make decisions, drawing on decades of psychological research. Kahneman describes two mental systems: a fast, intuitive one that handles most everyday choices, and a slower, more deliberate one that we use only when we have to. The interesting part is how often the fast system leads us astray — confirming what we already believe, anchoring on irrelevant numbers, judging probabilities by how easily an example comes to mind.

What made the book so influential for me was that it changed how I evaluate my own thinking. After reading it, I started noticing the small mental shortcuts I take dozens of times a day, particularly when I'm tired or under pressure. I became much more sceptical of strong intuitions, especially in areas where I have no real expertise, and I started building in more deliberate pauses before decisions that matter — when I'm hiring someone, for example, or making a financial choice.

It's not a self-help book at all, and it doesn't pretend to give you tricks to think better. But it broadened my perspective on what 'rational thinking' actually requires. I'd genuinely recommend it to anyone who has to make important decisions, which is more or less everyone.
keyPhrases: what made the book so influential

samples.prompt: Describe a memorable meal you had. You should say: where you had it, who you were with, what you ate, and explain why this meal was memorable.
samples.modelAnswer:
A meal I still think about quite often was a dinner I had with my sister and her husband at a small family-run restaurant in a hill town in northern Italy, about four years ago. We'd been driving through the region for a week and stumbled onto the place almost by accident — it had no website, no obvious sign, just a tiny doorway with a hand-painted menu beside it.

There were probably six tables inside, and an older woman who turned out to be both the cook and the owner. She brought out four courses without us really ordering — a plate of cured meats from the valley, a fresh egg pasta with butter and aged cheese, a slow-braised lamb dish with a sauce that I still cannot describe properly, and a simple lemon tart with espresso to finish. None of it was elaborate, but every single element was precisely what it should have been.

What made the meal memorable wasn't just the food, though. It was the whole atmosphere — the unrushed pace, the conversation between the three of us drifting from family stories to plans for the next day, the fact that the owner sat down with us for ten minutes after the dessert and told us about her grandmother, who had run the same restaurant decades earlier.

Looking back, it's etched in my memory partly because of the food and partly because it captured something about how meals are meant to be — slow, generous, shared with people you care about. I think about it often when I find myself eating quickly at my desk.
keyPhrases: precisely what it should have been

samples.prompt: Describe a teacher who had a strong influence on you. You should say: who they were, what subject they taught, what their teaching style was, and explain how they influenced you.
samples.modelAnswer:
The teacher I'd like to talk about is a woman called Ms Carter who taught me history when I was around fourteen or fifteen. On paper, she taught a fairly conventional curriculum, but the way she ran her classroom was different from anyone else I'd had before or since.

Her style was almost entirely Socratic. She'd come into the room, write a single open question on the board — something like, 'Was the Industrial Revolution good or bad for ordinary people?' — and then she'd sit on the corner of her desk and wait. She refused to lecture for more than about ten minutes at a stretch, because she said her job wasn't to tell us what she thought, it was to push us to think clearly. If you gave a lazy answer, she'd ask, very politely, 'And what's the evidence for that?' If you said something interesting, she'd follow up with three more questions until you either developed your argument properly or admitted you needed to reconsider.

There's one specific moment I remember vividly. I'd written an essay arguing some sweeping generalisation about colonialism, and instead of just marking it, she handed it back with a single note: 'Argue with yourself for the next paragraph.' That instruction has genuinely shaped how I write and think to this day — the habit of taking my own arguments and trying to break them before someone else does.

The lasting influence is hard to overstate. She convinced me that careful thinking is a skill, not a personality trait, and that anyone can develop it with enough patience. I still hear her voice when I'm tempted to settle for a half-answer.

samples.prompt: Describe a piece of technology you find useful in your daily life. You should say: what it is, how often you use it, what you use it for, and explain why it is so useful.
samples.modelAnswer:
The piece of technology I rely on most is something fairly unglamorous — a basic e-reader, in my case a Kindle Paperwhite that I've had for about three years.

I use it almost every day. On weekday mornings I read on it during my commute, in the evenings I usually have it open for half an hour before bed, and on weekends I tend to read for longer stretches. Over the course of a typical week I'd guess I spend something like eight or ten hours with it.

The obvious use is just reading books. I tend to switch between non-fiction during weekdays and longer novels at weekends. Beyond that, I use it for highlighting passages — when I find a sentence that stops me, I mark it, and the device keeps a clean list I can review later. I've also used the built-in dictionary more than I expected, particularly for older books with unfamiliar vocabulary.

What makes it indispensable, though, isn't really any single feature. It's the fact that the screen is genuinely comfortable to read for long periods, that it doesn't notify me about anything, and that the battery lasts a fortnight. In a world that's full of devices competing for my attention, having one piece of technology that does only one thing, and does it well, has been quietly transformative. I read significantly more now than I did before I owned one — probably twice as many books a year — and the time spent on it doesn't carry the slightly hollow feeling that comes with too much time on a phone.

samples.prompt: Describe a difficult decision you had to make. You should say: what the decision was, when you made it, what factors you considered, and explain how you felt about it afterwards.
samples.modelAnswer:
A genuinely difficult decision I made was leaving a job I liked quite a lot, about three years ago, to take a more uncertain role at a much smaller company. On paper, the decision should have been straightforward — the new role had a better title, slightly more responsibility, and the chance to work on something I cared about more deeply — but in practice it took me weeks to settle on it.

What made it hard was the trade-off. The existing job was stable, well-paid, and full of colleagues I genuinely enjoyed working with. The new one was at a company that was three years old, with a small team and no guarantee of being around in another three. I had to weigh up security and friendship on one side against the chance to do work I'd find more meaningful on the other, and there wasn't an obvious right answer.

I talked it through with people whose judgement I trust — my partner, a former mentor, a friend who'd made a similar move years earlier — and I made lists of the considerations, which felt slightly silly but actually helped clarify what I cared about most. In the end, I decided that I'd regret not taking the risk more than I'd regret taking it and having it not work out.

In hindsight, it turned out to be the right call. The smaller company has done well, and the work has been more interesting than I expected. But honestly, even if it hadn't, I think I'd still feel the decision-making process was sound. You can't judge a decision purely by its outcome.

samples.prompt: Describe a habit you have changed in your life. You should say: what the habit was, how you changed it, how long the change has lasted, and explain how the change has affected you.
samples.modelAnswer:
A habit I'm genuinely glad I changed is the way I used to spend the first hour of every morning. For years, the first thing I'd do when I woke up was reach for my phone, scroll through messages, glance at the news, and then somehow lose another twenty minutes before I'd even got out of bed. It set a kind of distracted, slightly anxious tone for the rest of the day.

About eighteen months ago I decided to try something different. The change itself was simple — I left my phone on a shelf in the next room overnight, and bought a small alarm clock for under twenty pounds — but the effect was bigger than I expected. Suddenly there was nothing to scroll, so I started actually getting up. I'd make coffee, sit by the window for ten or fifteen minutes with whatever book I was reading, and then begin the day from a calmer place.

The change has lasted, more or less. There have been a few weeks where the old habit crept back in — usually during stressful periods at work — but each time I've managed to reset within a few days, partly because I now know how much better the alternative feels.

What surprised me was the knock-on effect. The change wasn't just about avoiding the phone in the morning; it gradually shifted how I used it later in the day too. I check it less often, I'm more deliberate about what I open, and I sleep better because I'm not scrolling in bed at night either. Honestly, it's been one of the higher-return decisions I've made.
keyPhrases: the effect was bigger than I expected

samples.prompt: Part 3 follow-up discussion: How do you think individual behaviour change compares with government policy in addressing environmental problems? Should companies be required to publish their environmental impact? Are younger generations more environmentally conscious than older ones, and if so, why?
structure: take a clear position on each sub-question
samples.modelAnswer:
On the first question — I'd argue that individual action and government policy are complementary rather than alternatives. Individual behaviour matters because it shifts consumer demand, which signals to companies what's worth producing. But unless governments set the rules — emissions standards, energy market design, building regulations — even significant individual effort gets overwhelmed by structural inertia. Policy is the multiplier; behaviour is the seed.

On the second — yes, I think large companies should be required to publish standardised data on their environmental impact, in the same way they publish financial statements. The problem at the moment is that voluntary disclosure rewards companies that are good at marketing rather than those genuinely doing better. Mandatory, audited reporting puts everyone on the same scoreboard. Smaller companies probably need a lighter version of the same rules so the compliance burden isn't disproportionate.

On the third — there's clearly something to the idea that younger generations care more, but I'd be careful with it. Younger people grew up with the issue front and centre in their education, and they have most of their adult lives ahead of them in the world we're shaping, so they have more skin in the game. But they're also often the people with the least power to do anything about it. Older generations include the policymakers, the executives and the senior voters whose choices have far more leverage. So I'd reframe it: it's less that younger people are uniquely conscious and more that the responsibility is unevenly distributed.

samples.prompt: Part 3 follow-up discussion: Why do some people change jobs frequently while others stay in the same role for decades? Is it better for the economy if employees stay long-term with one employer? How might the nature of work change in the next twenty years?
structure: address each sub-question with a clear position
samples.modelAnswer:
On the first — the reasons divide roughly into three categories. Some people change jobs frequently because their skills are highly portable and the market rewards each move with better pay or seniority — this is common in software and finance. Others change frequently because their initial choices weren't a good fit and they're still searching. And then a third group stay long-term because they value the depth that comes from really understanding one organisation, or because their work is highly specialised and the available roles are few. Both patterns can produce strong careers; they suit different temperaments.

On the second — there's a balance. Long tenures are good for tacit knowledge, mentorship and institutional memory, all of which matter more than people often realise. But too little labour mobility can also calcify organisations, and economies with very low job switching tend to have weaker wage growth, because workers don't benefit from competition for their skills. The ideal is probably moderate mobility — enough that talent flows to where it's most useful, but not so much that no one stays long enough to develop deep expertise.

On the third — over the next two decades, the most significant change is likely to be the redistribution of tasks rather than the disappearance of jobs. Many routine analytical tasks will be automated, but human judgement, supervision and relationship work will become more valuable, not less. The skills people will need are probably the ones that are hardest to automate: defining problems clearly, working across disciplines and managing ambiguity. Education systems are not yet adapted to that, but they will have to be.
